To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the two Tn10 ends interact during transposition, that cleavage at one end can occur before cleavage at the other end, and that mutations in the three terminal base pairs of Tn10 affect steps of transposition subsequent to interaction of the ends.

Tn10 transposase cleaves at the two transposition ends at observably distinct stages during the transposition pathway, and that the three terminal base pairs of Tn10 have roles subsequent to interaction of the two ends.

Tn10 transposase cleaves at both ends of the transposon prior to integration and that the two cleavages are temporally separated, with cleavage at one end occurring before cleavage at the other end, even when both ends are in an interaction complex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the temporal and spatial organization of Tn10 transpositional reactions, and with the roles of terminal base pairs during the course of those reactions.
the mechanisms of transposition and the roles of specific basepairs during transposition.
the temporal order of events during transposon transposition in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ends of Tn10 interact in vivo, subsequent to which the element undergoes double strand cleavage(s) at each end, and the terminal basepairs are important in the chemical steps or positioning of residues or the coupling of cleavages to subsequent conformation changes.
the terminal basepairs are involved in multiple aspects of Tn10 transpositional events subsequent to the initial interaction of ends.
the ends of the Tn10 transposon must interact for cleavage of either end, and that cleavage of one end can occur at a distinct time prior to cleavage of the other end.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Tn10 transposon ends can interact with one another to facilitate double strand cleavage(s) at either end, but the time between cleavage(s) and strand transfer is variable, and the three terminal bp of Tn10 are important for the chemistry and/or conformational changes of transposition.
the terminal basepairs of a transposon end can play multiple roles during transposition.
Tn10 transposase is a ‘‘two‐ended’’ enzyme that acts on a single transposon end to promote cleavage of that end, and then acts on the second end to promote cleavages at that end.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Tn10 transposase can catalyze double strand cleavage(s) and/or strand transfer at one or both ends of the element in the absence of cleavage(s)/strand transfer at the other end(s).
Tn10 transposon ends interact prior to cleavage at either of them.
the two ends of Tn10 can interact with one another prior to double strand cleavage(s) at either end, and that this interaction of ends is required for cleavage at either or both ends.
